newsitem.title: USA: Near-term U.S. soybean crush seen strong - analysts.
newsitem.headline: Near-term U.S. soybean crush seen strong - analysts.

text.p: The strong pace of the U.S. soybean crush is expected to continue through the middle of March, when exports from South America should slice into demand for U.S. soy products, grain analysts said.
"We're not going to see any significant reduction in this crush until the Southern Hemisphere comes on stream," said Dale Gustafson, grain analyst with Smith Barney in Chicago.

The National Oilseed Processors Association on Thursday reported a weekly crush of 30.335 million bushels versus 29.697 million a week ago. The crush was at the high end of trade estimates, but most had anticipated a robust pace.
The weekly soybean crushing pace will continue to hover around 29 to 30 million bushels before falling back near last year's pace toward the end of March, Gustafson forecast.

Since September, the U.S. monthly crush has been on a steady climb and has remained well above year-ago levels, according to monthly crushing data from the U.S. Census Bureau. The bureau reported that 138.2 million bushels of soybeans were crushed in December, up from 125.0 million in December, 1995.
Analysts said the increase has been fueled primarily by an active U.S. soymeal export program.
"Domestic demand has been steady, but more and more processors I've talked to said they can still go to the river and sell their meal (for export)," one soymeal broker said.

But those exports will slow dramatically when the new soybean crop from Brazil is harvested and begins to filter into world export markets in approximately 30 to 45 days, cash traders and analysts said.
Both the Brazilian and Argentine soybean crops are forecast to be larger than last year's, and both nations are committed to aggressively exporting oilseeds.
Aside from the record crop, Brazilian exports are likely to grow in 1997 because of a new law that essentially scraps the tax on exports of raw materials, cash sources said.
"With the tariff relief on their exports, you can bet they're going to export heavily," one cash soymeal broker said.
Another factor that will contribute to a slowing of the U.S. crushing pace would be the fact that U.S. soybean supplies are so tight, analysts said.
In its last supply and demand report, the U.S. Department of Agriculture estimated 1996/97 soybean ending stocks at 155 million bushels, down from the previous estimate of 180 million.
"Eventually, they are going to have to slow down," said Dan Cekander, grain analyst with FIMAT Futures Inc brokerage in Chicago. "If the beans aren't there, you just literally can't crush them."
Despite the forecasts for a slowdown in the historically high pace of the U.S. crush, analysts do not see any dramatic cutbacks because world demand for protein continues to grow, they said.
